question_html: As defined in section 2(13) of the Companies Act, 2013, what records are included within the meaning of 'books of account'?

options.A: Records maintained in respect of all sums of money received and expended by a company and matters relating to such receipts and expenditure; all sales and purchases of goods and services by the company; the assets and liabilities of the company; and, for a company belonging to a class specified under section 148, the items of cost prescribed under that section
options.B: Records maintained exclusively in respect of the company's fixed assets register, to the express exclusion of any record of sums of money received and expended, or of sales and purchases of goods and services
options.C: Records maintained exclusively in respect of minutes of Board and general meetings, deeds, vouchers, and registers - this being the statutory meaning of 'book and paper' under section 2(12), not of 'books of account' under section 2(13)
options.D: Records maintained exclusively in respect of the company's tax filings and statutory returns submitted to the Income-tax authorities, to the exclusion of internal receipts, expenditure, sales, purchases, assets, or liabilities

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Records maintained in respect of all sums of money received and expended by a company and matters relating to such receipts and expenditure; all sales and purchases of goods and services by the company; the assets and liabilities of the company; and, for a company belonging to a class specified under section 148, the items of cost prescribed under that section

Section 2(13) defines 'books of account' inclusively to cover records of all sums received/expended (and related matters), all sales/purchases of goods and services, the assets and liabilities of the company, and (for companies covered under section 148) prescribed items of cost - a broader concept than 'book and paper' under section 2(12), which separately covers books of account, deeds, vouchers, writings, documents, minutes, and registers.

question_html: Under section 128(1), what two accounting requirements must a company's books of account satisfy, and can a company validly maintain its books under the single-entry system or on cash basis instead?

options.A: Section 128(1) permits a company to choose freely between cash basis and accrual basis of accounting, and between single-entry and double-entry systems, depending on the size and nature of its business, without any statutory preference for either
options.B: Section 128(1) requires the books of account to give a true and fair view of the state of affairs of the company (including its branches) and to be kept on ACCRUAL basis and according to the DOUBLE-ENTRY system of accounting; no exception is given to any class of companies from this requirement, so a company cannot validly maintain its books on cash basis or under the single-entry system
options.C: Section 128(1) requires books of account to be kept strictly on cash basis and under the single-entry system, since accrual accounting and double-entry bookkeeping are permitted only for listed companies under a separate SEBI regulation
options.D: Section 128(1) permits small companies and one person companies (but no other class of company) to maintain books of account under the single-entry system, on cash basis, as a simplification measure

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Section 128(1) requires the books of account to give a true and fair view of the state of affairs of the company (including its branches) and to be kept on ACCRUAL basis and according to the DOUBLE-ENTRY system of accounting; no exception is given to any class of companies from this requirement, so a company cannot validly maintain its books on cash basis or under the single-entry system

Section 128(1) mandates that books of account give a true and fair view of the company's affairs (including branches) and be kept on accrual basis and according to the double-entry system of accounting - with no exception carved out for any class of companies, so single-entry or cash-basis accounting is impermissible for every company, regardless of size.

question_html: What do the concepts of 'true and fair view' and 'accrual basis of accounting' mean in the context of section 128(1)?

options.A: 'True and fair view' means the financial statements are certified as error-free in every respect by the statutory auditor, and 'accrual basis' means recording income and expenses only when cash is actually received or paid, making it synonymous with the cash system
options.B: 'True and fair view' refers exclusively to compliance with tax laws (rather than accounting standards), and 'accrual basis' refers to a system under which only expenses (and never income) are recorded before actual receipt or payment
options.C: 'True and fair view of the state of affairs' means the financial statements are free from material misstatements and faithfully represent the financial performance and positioning of the entity; 'accrual basis of accounting' is an accounting concept that warrants recording income and expenses as they accrue (are earned or incurred) - as opposed to the cash system, where they are recorded only when actually received or paid
options.D: 'True and fair view' and 'accrual basis' are two names for the identical accounting concept under section 128(1), used interchangeably by the Companies Act, 2013, with no distinct meaning attributable to either term

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) 'True and fair view of the state of affairs' means the financial statements are free from material misstatements and faithfully represent the financial performance and positioning of the entity; 'accrual basis of accounting' is an accounting concept that warrants recording income and expenses as they accrue (are earned or incurred) - as opposed to the cash system, where they are recorded only when actually received or paid

'True and fair view' signifies financial statements free from material misstatement, faithfully representing financial performance and position; 'accrual basis of accounting' is the concept of recording income and expenses as they accrue (earned/incurred), in contrast to the cash system, which records them only on actual receipt/payment - both concepts are distinct and both are mandated by section 128(1).

question_html: Can a company keep all or any of its books of account at a place other than its registered office, and if so, what compliance step follows such a decision?

options.A: No - section 128(1) mandates that books of account be kept exclusively at the company's registered office, with no power vested in the Board of Directors (or any other authority) to decide otherwise, under any circumstances
options.B: Yes - the Board of Directors may decide to keep books of account at any place, whether within India or outside India, without any obligation to notify the Registrar of such a decision at any time
options.C: Yes - but such a decision requires the prior approval of the Registrar of Companies before it can be implemented, rather than merely notifying the Registrar in Form AOC-5 within seven days after the decision is taken
options.D: Yes - the First Proviso to section 128(1) permits all or any of the books of account to be kept at such other place in India as the Board of Directors may decide; where such a decision is taken, the company shall, within seven days thereof, file with the Registrar a notice in writing in Form AOC-5 (per Rule 2A of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014) giving the full address of that other place

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Yes - the First Proviso to section 128(1) permits all or any of the books of account to be kept at such other place in India as the Board of Directors may decide; where such a decision is taken, the company shall, within seven days thereof, file with the Registrar a notice in writing in Form AOC-5 (per Rule 2A of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014) giving the full address of that other place

The First Proviso to section 128(1) allows books of account to be kept at any other place in India that the Board decides - but confines this power to a place within India (not outside), and requires notice in Form AOC-5 to be filed with the Registrar within 7 days of the Board's decision, giving the full address of that place.

question_html: For a company using accounting software to maintain its books of account, what does the proviso to Rule 3(1) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 require, and from which financial year does this requirement apply?

options.A: For the financial year commencing on or after 1st April 2023, every such company shall use only accounting software that has a feature of recording an audit trail of each and every transaction, creating an edit log of each change made in the books of account (along with the date of such change), and ensuring that the audit trail CANNOT be disabled
options.B: The audit trail requirement applies only to listed companies, and only for the financial year commencing on or after 1st April 2023, with no such requirement extending to any unlisted company using accounting software
options.C: The proviso permits a company to disable the audit trail feature at its discretion, provided the company discloses in its Board's report that the feature has been disabled for a stated business reason
options.D: The audit trail and edit log requirement applies retrospectively to all financial years, including those commencing before 1st April 2023, without any specific effective date being prescribed under Rule 3(1)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) For the financial year commencing on or after 1st April 2023, every such company shall use only accounting software that has a feature of recording an audit trail of each and every transaction, creating an edit log of each change made in the books of account (along with the date of such change), and ensuring that the audit trail CANNOT be disabled

The proviso to Rule 3(1) requires that, for the financial year commencing on or after 1st April 2023, every company using accounting software for its books of account must use only software with an audit-trail feature recording every transaction, an edit log of every change (with the date of change), and must ensure this audit trail cannot be disabled - a requirement applying to companies generally, not merely listed companies.

question_html: Where a company maintains its books of account in electronic mode, including at a place outside India, what does the proviso to Rule 3(5) require regarding back-up of such records?

options.A: The back-up of electronically maintained books of account need only be kept on servers located in India on an ANNUAL basis, coinciding with the filing of the company's financial statements with the Registrar
options.B: The back-up of the books of account and other books and papers of the company maintained in electronic mode, including at a place outside India (if any), shall be kept in servers physically located in India, on a DAILY basis
options.C: There is no requirement at all to keep any back-up of books of account maintained in electronic mode within India; back-up may be maintained exclusively on servers located outside India, wherever the company's service provider is based
options.D: The back-up of electronically maintained books of account must be kept on servers located in India on a QUARTERLY basis, aligning with the periodicity prescribed for summarised returns from branch offices under Rule 4(1)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The back-up of the books of account and other books and papers of the company maintained in electronic mode, including at a place outside India (if any), shall be kept in servers physically located in India, on a DAILY basis

The proviso to Rule 3(5) mandates that back-up of the electronically maintained books of account and other books/papers - including any maintained at a place outside India - must be kept in servers physically located in India, and this back-up must be taken on a DAILY basis, ensuring data resiliency and accessibility within India at all times.

question_html: Where a company has a branch office in or outside India, when is it deemed to have complied with section 128(1) in respect of that branch, and at what interval must summarised returns be sent to the registered office?

options.A: A company is deemed to have complied with section 128(1) only if the branch office's books of account are physically transferred in original to the registered office at the end of every financial year, rather than being kept at the branch office itself with periodic summarised returns
options.B: Summarised returns from a branch office maintaining books outside India must be sent to the registered office on a MONTHLY basis (not quarterly), per Rule 4(1) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014
options.C: A company is deemed to have complied with section 128(1) if proper books of account relating to transactions at the branch office are kept at that office, and proper summarised returns are periodically sent by the branch to the company's registered office (or other place under sub-section 1); per Rule 4(1), such summarised returns (for books kept outside India) shall be sent to the registered office at QUARTERLY intervals, and kept open for inspection by directors
options.D: A company is deemed to have complied with section 128(1) in respect of a branch office only if it appoints a separate statutory auditor exclusively for that branch, distinct from the auditor appointed for the company as a whole

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) A company is deemed to have complied with section 128(1) if proper books of account relating to transactions at the branch office are kept at that office, and proper summarised returns are periodically sent by the branch to the company's registered office (or other place under sub-section 1); per Rule 4(1), such summarised returns (for books kept outside India) shall be sent to the registered office at QUARTERLY intervals, and kept open for inspection by directors

Section 128(2) deems compliance where proper branch books are kept at the branch and proper summarised returns are periodically sent to the registered office; Rule 4(1) specifies that such summarised returns (in respect of books kept outside India) must be sent QUARTERLY, and must be kept and maintained at the registered office, open for inspection by directors.

question_html: How does a director's right to inspect books of account maintained WITHIN India differ from his right to obtain financial information maintained OUTSIDE the country, in terms of procedure and timeline?

options.A: A director enjoys an identical, unrestricted right of inspection for both India-based books and financial information maintained outside the country, with no written request or fifteen-day timeline applicable to either category
options.B: For financial information maintained outside the country, the director's power of attorney holder, agent, or representative may make the written request on the director's behalf, exactly as the director himself could
options.C: The company must produce financial information maintained outside the country to the requesting director within THIRTY DAYS (not fifteen days) of receipt of his written request, per Rule 4(3) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014
options.D: Any director can inspect books of account and other books/papers maintained WITHIN India during business hours, without any special procedure; but for financial information maintained OUTSIDE the country, the director must furnish a written request (setting out full details of the information sought and the period for which it is sought) under Rule 4(2), and the company must produce such information to the director within FIFTEEN DAYS of receipt of that written request under Rule 4(3)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Any director can inspect books of account and other books/papers maintained WITHIN India during business hours, without any special procedure; but for financial information maintained OUTSIDE the country, the director must furnish a written request (setting out full details of the information sought and the period for which it is sought) under Rule 4(2), and the company must produce such information to the director within FIFTEEN DAYS of receipt of that written request under Rule 4(3)

Inspection of India-based books is unrestricted (any director, during business hours), while financial information maintained outside the country requires a written request under Rule 4(2) (detailing the information sought and the period), with the company bound to produce it within 15 days under Rule 4(3) - and the Study Material notes this request must be made by the director himself, not through a power of attorney holder, agent, or representative.

question_html: For how long must books of account (together with relevant vouchers) be preserved under section 128(5), and what penalty applies under section 128(6) for contravention by the responsible officers?

options.A: Books of account, together with vouchers relevant to any entry in such books, must be preserved in good order for a period of not less than EIGHT YEARS immediately preceding the relevant financial year (subject to a longer period if directed by the Central Government where an investigation has been ordered); the managing director, whole-time director in charge of finance, Chief Financial Officer, or other person charged with this duty, upon contravention, is punishable with a fine of not less than Rs. 50,000 but which may extend to Rs. 5 lakh
options.B: Books of account must be preserved for a period of not less than five years (rather than eight years) immediately preceding the relevant financial year, and no penalty at all is prescribed under section 128(6) for contravention by responsible officers
options.C: Vouchers relevant to entries in the books of account need not be preserved at all as part of the 8-year preservation requirement; only the books of account themselves (excluding vouchers) must be so preserved
options.D: The penalty prescribed under section 128(6) for contravention is imprisonment of up to two years, with no monetary fine component, applicable exclusively to the managing director and to no other officer of the company

answer_html:

question_html: As per section 2(40), what does the term 'financial statement' include in relation to a company, and is a cash flow statement mandatory for every company without exception?

options.A: 'Financial statement' includes only the balance sheet and profit and loss account; a cash flow statement and statement of changes in equity are never included within the meaning of 'financial statement' under section 2(40), for any company
options.B: 'Financial statement' includes a balance sheet as at the end of the financial year; a profit and loss account (or income and expenditure account for a not-for-profit company); a cash flow statement for the financial year; a statement of changes in equity, if applicable; and any explanatory note annexed to or forming part of the above - but a cash flow statement is NOT mandatory for a one person company, small company, dormant company, and a private company that is a start-up (and has not defaulted in filing financial statements/annual return), per the relevant exemption notification
options.C: A cash flow statement is mandatory for every company without exception, including one person companies, small companies, dormant companies, and start-up private companies, since section 2(40) provides no carve-out from this requirement
options.D: 'Financial statement' under section 2(40) refers exclusively to the consolidated financial statement of a company having subsidiaries; a company without any subsidiary is not considered to have a 'financial statement' at all under this definition

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) 'Financial statement' includes a balance sheet as at the end of the financial year; a profit and loss account (or income and expenditure account for a not-for-profit company); a cash flow statement for the financial year; a statement of changes in equity, if applicable; and any explanatory note annexed to or forming part of the above - but a cash flow statement is NOT mandatory for a one person company, small company, dormant company, and a private company that is a start-up (and has not defaulted in filing financial statements/annual return), per the relevant exemption notification

question_html: For an insurance company, banking company, or a company engaged in generation/supply of electricity, does the financial statement fail to present a 'true and fair view' merely because it does not disclose matters not required to be disclosed by the sector-specific governing law (e.g., the Insurance Act, 1938 or the Banking Regulation Act, 1949)?

options.A: Yes - such companies' financial statements are automatically treated as failing to present a true and fair view whenever any matter not required by the sector-specific Act remains undisclosed, regardless of compliance with that sector-specific Act
options.B: No - but this exception applies only to insurance and banking companies, and does NOT extend to companies engaged in the generation or supply of electricity, or to companies governed by any other special Act
options.C: No - the financial statements of such specified companies (insurance, banking, or electricity generation/supply companies, or a company governed by any other law requiring a specific form of financial statement) shall NOT be treated as failing to disclose a true and fair view of the state of affairs, merely by reason of not disclosing matters that are not required to be disclosed by the relevant sector-specific Act
options.D: Yes, but only for insurance companies specifically; for banking companies and companies engaged in generation/supply of electricity, non-disclosure of sector-specific-law-exempted matters DOES compromise the true-and-fair-view standard

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) No - the financial statements of such specified companies (insurance, banking, or electricity generation/supply companies, or a company governed by any other law requiring a specific form of financial statement) shall NOT be treated as failing to disclose a true and fair view of the state of affairs, merely by reason of not disclosing matters that are not required to be disclosed by the relevant sector-specific Act

The proviso to section 129(1) makes clear that non-disclosure of matters not required to be disclosed under the applicable sector-specific law (Insurance Act 1938/IRDA Act 1999 for insurance companies, Banking Regulation Act 1949 for banking companies, Electricity Act 2003 for electricity companies, or any other governing law) does not, by itself, mean the financial statements fail to present a true and fair view - this protection extends across all four listed categories, not merely insurance companies.

question_html: To which classes of company does sub-section (1) of section 129 (requiring compliance with the form(s) in Schedule III) NOT apply, and how many divisions does Schedule III carry for financial statement formats?

options.A: Section 129(1) applies without exception to every class of company, including insurance, banking, and electricity-generation companies; Schedule III carries only a single, undivided format applicable uniformly to all companies
options.B: Schedule III carries TWO divisions only - one for listed companies and one for unlisted companies - and section 129(1) does not apply to any company having a paid-up share capital exceeding rupees ten crore
options.C: Section 129(1) does not apply solely to insurance companies (and no other sectoral category); Schedule III carries FOUR divisions, the fourth being reserved specifically for Government companies

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Section 129(1) does not apply to an insurance company, a banking company, a company engaged in the generation or supply of electricity, or any other class of company for which a form of financial statement has been specified in or under the Act governing such class of company; Schedule III carries THREE divisions - Division I (Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021 compliant companies), Division II (non-NBFC companies complying with Ind AS), and Division III (NBFCs complying with Ind AS)

question_html: Where a company has one or more subsidiaries or associate companies, what additional financial statement must it prepare, in what form, and where must it be laid?

options.A: In addition to its own financial statements under sub-section (2), the company shall prepare a Consolidated Financial Statement (CFS) of the company and of all its subsidiaries, associate companies, and joint ventures, in the same form and manner as its own financial statements and in accordance with applicable accounting standards, and this CFS shall also be laid before the Annual General Meeting of the company along with the laying of its own financial statement
options.B: A company having one or more subsidiaries or associate companies is required to prepare a consolidated financial statement only if it is a listed company; unlisted companies with subsidiaries or associates are entirely exempt from this requirement under section 129(3)
options.C: The consolidated financial statement, once prepared, need not be laid before the Annual General Meeting at all; it need only be filed directly with the Registrar, bypassing the AGM-laying requirement applicable to the company's own (standalone) financial statement
options.D: A company is required to prepare a consolidated financial statement only in respect of its subsidiaries; associate companies and joint ventures are entirely excluded from the scope of consolidation required under section 129(3)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) In addition to its own financial statements under sub-section (2), the company shall prepare a Consolidated Financial Statement (CFS) of the company and of all its subsidiaries, associate companies, and joint ventures, in the same form and manner as its own financial statements and in accordance with applicable accounting standards, and this CFS shall also be laid before the Annual General Meeting of the company along with the laying of its own financial statement

Section 129(3) requires a company with one or more subsidiaries or associate companies to prepare a Consolidated Financial Statement (CFS) covering the company and ALL its subsidiaries, associate companies, and joint ventures - in the same form/manner as its own statements and per applicable accounting standards - and to lay this CFS before the AGM alongside its own financial statement, irrespective of listing status.

question_html: Under what THREE cumulative conditions is a company exempted from preparing consolidated financial statements, even though it has one or more subsidiaries?

options.A: A company is exempted from preparing CFS if it satisfies ANY ONE (rather than all three) of the listed conditions - being a wholly/partially owned subsidiary, having unlisted securities, or having a holding company that files CFS - since the conditions operate independently of each other
options.B: (a) It is a wholly owned subsidiary, or a partially owned subsidiary whose other members (including non-voting members), after being intimated in writing with proof of delivery available, do not object to non-presentation of CFS; (b) its securities are not listed, and are not in the process of listing, on any stock exchange in or outside India; and (c) its ultimate or any intermediate holding company files consolidated financial statements with the Registrar that comply with the applicable Accounting Standards - ALL THREE conditions must be satisfied together
options.C: A company is exempted from preparing CFS solely on the ground that it is a wholly owned subsidiary, with no further condition relating to listing status or the holding company's own CFS-filing compliance being relevant to the exemption
options.D: A company is exempted from preparing CFS only if its ultimate holding company is incorporated outside India; a company whose ultimate holding company is incorporated in India can never claim this exemption, regardless of its own listing status or ownership structure

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) (a) It is a wholly owned subsidiary, or a partially owned subsidiary whose other members (including non-voting members), after being intimated in writing with proof of delivery available, do not object to non-presentation of CFS; (b) its securities are not listed, and are not in the process of listing, on any stock exchange in or outside India; and (c) its ultimate or any intermediate holding company files consolidated financial statements with the Registrar that comply with the applicable Accounting Standards - ALL THREE conditions must be satisfied together

The exemption from preparing CFS applies only where ALL three conditions are cumulatively satisfied: the specific wholly/partially-owned-subsidiary-with-no-member-objection condition, the unlisted-securities condition, and the ultimate/intermediate-holding-company-files-compliant-CFS condition - a company failing even one of these three conditions remains obligated to prepare its own consolidated financial statement.

options.A: The company need only disclose the deviation from the accounting standards; disclosure of the reasons for such deviation and of the financial effects arising from it are optional, left to the company's discretion under section 129(5)
options.B: The company must disclose the deviation and the reasons for such deviation, but is expressly exempted from disclosing the financial effects (if any) arising out of such deviation, under section 129(5)

question_html: If it appears to the directors of a company that its financial statements do not comply with section 129, or its Board's report does not comply with section 134, what may they do, and what procedural steps under section 131(1) must be followed?

options.A: The revisions may extend to any matter whatsoever that the directors consider appropriate to update or improve, with no confinement at all to correcting non-compliance with sections 129 or 134, once Tribunal approval for revision has been obtained
options.B: The revisions must be confined exclusively to correcting arithmetical errors in the financial statement; corrections relating to non-compliance with the substantive requirements of sections 129 or 134 are outside the scope of permitted revision under section 131(2)
options.C: The revisions must be confined exclusively to updating the auditor's report attached to the financial statement, since section 131(2) governs revision of the auditor's report rather than the financial statement or Board's report itself

question_html: Under Rule 3 of the National Financial Reporting Authority Rules, 2018, which of the following categories of company falls within NFRA's oversight for monitoring and enforcing compliance with accounting and auditing standards?

options.A: Companies whose securities are listed on any stock exchange in India or outside India; unlisted public companies having paid-up capital of not less than Rs. 500 crore, OR annual turnover of not less than Rs. 1,000 crore, OR aggregate outstanding loans, debentures, and deposits of not less than Rs. 500 crore as on 31st March of the immediately preceding financial year; insurance/banking/electricity companies and bodies corporate incorporated by a special Act; entities referred to NFRA by the Central Government in public interest; and certain foreign subsidiaries/associates meeting an income/net-worth threshold
options.B: NFRA's oversight is confined exclusively to companies whose securities are listed on a stock exchange in India; unlisted public companies (regardless of the size of their paid-up capital, turnover, or outstanding loans/deposits) fall entirely outside NFRA's jurisdiction under Rule 3
options.C: NFRA's oversight extends to every private company incorporated in India, regardless of its size, turnover, or paid-up capital, since Rule 3 makes no distinction between private and public companies
options.D: NFRA's oversight is confined exclusively to insurance, banking, and electricity companies; listed companies and large unlisted public companies fall outside NFRA's jurisdiction under Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018

question_html: What is the composition of the National Financial Reporting Authority, and what restriction applies to full-time Chairperson/members regarding association with audit firms?

options.A: NFRA consists solely of a Chairperson, with no other members at all, and there is no restriction whatsoever on the Chairperson's association with any audit firm, either during or after the tenure of appointment
options.B: NFRA consists of a Chairperson (a person of eminence with expertise in accountancy, auditing, finance, or law) and such other members, not exceeding FIFTEEN, consisting of part-time and full-time members; the Chairperson and members who are in full-time employment with NFRA shall NOT be associated with any audit firm (including related consultancy firms) during the course of their appointment AND for TWO YEARS after ceasing to hold such appointment
options.C: NFRA may have any number of members without any statutory ceiling, and the restriction on association with audit firms applies only during the course of appointment, ending immediately upon ceasing to hold office (with no post-tenure cooling-off period)
options.D: The restriction on association with audit firms applies only to part-time members of NFRA (and not to the Chairperson or full-time members), and the cooling-off period after ceasing to hold appointment is one year (not two years)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) NFRA consists of a Chairperson (a person of eminence with expertise in accountancy, auditing, finance, or law) and such other members, not exceeding FIFTEEN, consisting of part-time and full-time members; the Chairperson and members who are in full-time employment with NFRA shall NOT be associated with any audit firm (including related consultancy firms) during the course of their appointment AND for TWO YEARS after ceasing to hold such appointment

NFRA's composition is capped at a Chairperson plus not more than 15 other members (part-time and full-time); full-time Chairperson/members are barred from association with any audit firm (including related consultancy firms) both during their appointment and for a two-year cooling-off period thereafter - a safeguard for independence given NFRA's oversight role over the audit profession.

question_html: Under section 132(4), into what matters may NFRA investigate, either suo motu or on reference from the Central Government, and what happens to proceedings by any OTHER institute or body once NFRA has initiated an investigation into the same matter?

options.A: NFRA may investigate professional misconduct only upon a reference made by the Central Government, and never suo motu on its own initiative, under section 132(4)
options.B: Once NFRA initiates an investigation into a matter of professional misconduct, the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) may nonetheless continue its own PARALLEL proceedings into the identical matter, since section 132(4) does not bar concurrent proceedings by ICAI
options.C: NFRA's power to investigate under section 132(4) extends only to matters of misconduct committed by companies (as legal entities), and not to misconduct committed by individual chartered accountants or firms of chartered accountants
options.D: NFRA has the power to investigate matters of professional or other misconduct committed by any member or firm of chartered accountants registered under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, either suo motu or on a reference made to it by the Central Government (per Rule 10 of the NFRA Rules, 2018); once NFRA has initiated an investigation under this section, no OTHER institute or body shall initiate or continue any proceedings in such matters of misconduct - section 132(4) has overriding effect over any other law for the time being in force

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) NFRA has the power to investigate matters of professional or other misconduct committed by any member or firm of chartered accountants registered under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, either suo motu or on a reference made to it by the Central Government (per Rule 10 of the NFRA Rules, 2018); once NFRA has initiated an investigation under this section, no OTHER institute or body shall initiate or continue any proceedings in such matters of misconduct - section 132(4) has overriding effect over any other law for the time being in force

Section 132(4) empowers NFRA to investigate professional/other misconduct by CA members/firms, whether suo motu or on Central Government reference, and this power has an OVERRIDING EFFECT - once NFRA initiates an investigation, no other institute or body (including, implicitly, ICAI's own disciplinary mechanism for that matter) may initiate or continue proceedings on the same matter, preventing parallel, duplicative proceedings.

question_html: Where professional or other misconduct is proved against an individual chartered accountant or a firm, what penalty and debarment period may NFRA order under section 132(4)(c)?

options.A: For an INDIVIDUAL: a penalty of not less than Rs. 1 lakh, but which may extend to FIVE TIMES the fees received; for a FIRM: a penalty of not less than Rs. 5 lakh, but which may extend to TEN TIMES the fees received; and in either case, NFRA may debar the member/firm from being appointed as an auditor/internal auditor (or undertaking any audit) or from performing a section 247 valuation, for a MINIMUM period of six months and a MAXIMUM period of ten years
options.B: For an individual, the penalty is a flat Rs. 5 lakh with no multiplier tied to fees received; for a firm, the penalty is a flat Rs. 10 lakh - and no debarment from acting as auditor is available under section 132(4)(c) in either case
options.C: The minimum and maximum debarment periods are identical for individuals and firms at a flat THREE years, with no minimum-six-months/maximum-ten-years range prescribed under section 132(4)(c)
options.D: The penalty for an individual may extend to TEN times the fees received (not five times), while the penalty for a firm may extend to FIVE times the fees received (not ten times) - i.e., the reverse of the correct individual/firm multiplier allocation

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) For an INDIVIDUAL: a penalty of not less than Rs. 1 lakh, but which may extend to FIVE TIMES the fees received; for a FIRM: a penalty of not less than Rs. 5 lakh, but which may extend to TEN TIMES the fees received; and in either case, NFRA may debar the member/firm from being appointed as an auditor/internal auditor (or undertaking any audit) or from performing a section 247 valuation, for a MINIMUM period of six months and a MAXIMUM period of ten years

Section 132(4)(c) fixes a fee-linked penalty range - Rs. 1 lakh to 5x fees for an individual, Rs. 5 lakh to 10x fees for a firm (the firm's minimum and multiplier both being higher, reflecting greater potential exposure) - together with a debarment power ranging from a minimum of 6 months to a maximum of 10 years, from acting as auditor/internal auditor or performing section 247 valuations.

question_html: If a person is aggrieved by an order of NFRA issued under clause (c) of section 132(4) (the penalty/debarment order), what recourse does section 132(5) provide?

options.A: An order of NFRA issued under clause (c) of section 132(4) is final and binding, with no right of appeal provided under the Companies Act, 2013, to any forum whatsoever
options.B: Any person aggrieved by such an order of NFRA may prefer an appeal before the APPELLATE TRIBUNAL, in such manner and on payment of such fee as may be prescribed

question_html: Before financial statements are submitted to the auditor for his report, by whom must they be approved and signed on behalf of the Board, per section 134(1), and how does this differ for a One Person Company?

options.A: The financial statements need be signed only by the company's statutory auditor, and no signature or approval is required from the chairperson, any director, the CEO, the CFO, or the company secretary, under section 134(1)
options.B: In every case, including a One Person Company, the financial statements must be signed by at least two directors, one of whom shall be the managing director, with no relaxation available for a One Person Company
options.C: The financial statements shall be approved by the Board and signed at least by: the chairperson of the company (where authorised by the Board) OR two directors (one of whom shall be the managing director, if any); the Chief Executive Officer; the Chief Financial Officer; and the company secretary (wherever appointed); in the case of a One Person Company, the financial statements shall be approved and signed by only ONE DIRECTOR
options.D: The financial statements need be signed only by the Chief Financial Officer, to the exclusion of the chairperson/directors, the Chief Executive Officer, and the company secretary, regardless of whether these officers have been appointed

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The financial statements shall be approved by the Board and signed at least by: the chairperson of the company (where authorised by the Board) OR two directors (one of whom shall be the managing director, if any); the Chief Executive Officer; the Chief Financial Officer; and the company secretary (wherever appointed); in the case of a One Person Company, the financial statements shall be approved and signed by only ONE DIRECTOR

Section 134(1) requires Board approval and signature by the chairperson (if Board-authorised) or two directors (one a managing director, if any), plus the CEO, CFO, and company secretary (wherever appointed) - but for a One Person Company, this multi-signatory requirement is relaxed to approval and signature by only ONE director, reflecting the OPC's single-director structure.

question_html: Can a company validly circulate UNAUDITED financial statements to its members before the Annual General Meeting, or file unaudited accounts with the Registrar?

options.A: Yes - a company may freely circulate unaudited financial statements to its members before the AGM, and may also file such unaudited accounts with the Registrar, since section 134 imposes no requirement to attach the auditor's report before circulation or filing
options.B: Yes, but only where the company's Articles of Association expressly permit circulation of unaudited accounts; absent such express permission in the Articles, circulation of unaudited accounts is barred under section 134(2)
options.C: No - circulation of unaudited accounts before the AGM is barred, but FILING of unaudited accounts with the Registrar is expressly permitted under section 134(7), provided the audited accounts are filed later as a supplement
options.D: No - section 134(2) requires the auditor's report to be attached to every financial statement, and section 134(7) requires a signed copy of every financial statement to be issued, circulated, or published along with the auditor's report (and the Board's report); it follows that unaudited accounts cannot be sent to members, nor can unaudited accounts be filed with the Registrar of Companies

answer_html:

question_html: By whom must the Board's report and any annexures thereto be signed, under section 134(6)?

question_html: What must the Directors' Responsibility Statement, referred to in section 134(3)(c), state regarding accounting standards, accounting policies, and the going concern basis of preparation?

options.A: The Directors' Responsibility Statement need state only that the accounts have been audited by a qualified chartered accountant, with no requirement to address accounting standards, accounting policies, adequate accounting records, or the going concern basis of preparation
options.B: The statement must state that: applicable accounting standards had been followed in preparing the annual accounts, with proper explanation for material departures; the directors had selected and consistently applied accounting policies, and made reasonable and prudent judgments/estimates, so as to give a true and fair view of the state of affairs and profit/loss for the period; the directors had taken proper and sufficient care for maintaining adequate accounting records (safeguarding assets, preventing/detecting fraud and irregularities); and the annual accounts had been prepared on a GOING CONCERN basis
options.C: The Directors' Responsibility Statement must state that the annual accounts have been prepared on a LIQUIDATION (rather than going concern) basis, reflecting the assumption that the company will be wound up within the following financial year
options.D: The Directors' Responsibility Statement is required only for listed companies; unlisted companies are entirely exempt from including any Directors' Responsibility Statement in their Board's report under section 134(3)(c)/(5)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The statement must state that: applicable accounting standards had been followed in preparing the annual accounts, with proper explanation for material departures; the directors had selected and consistently applied accounting policies, and made reasonable and prudent judgments/estimates, so as to give a true and fair view of the state of affairs and profit/loss for the period; the directors had taken proper and sufficient care for maintaining adequate accounting records (safeguarding assets, preventing/detecting fraud and irregularities); and the annual accounts had been prepared on a GOING CONCERN basis

question_html: For a LISTED company, what must the Directors' Responsibility Statement additionally state regarding internal financial controls, and can directors validly state that such controls are 'adequate and operating effectively' if a control failure occurred and was only later reinstated during the year?

options.A: A listed company's directors may validly state that internal financial controls are 'adequate and operating effectively' even where a failure occurred during the year, so long as the failure was reinstated before the financial year ended and the accounts were finalised
options.B: The internal-financial-controls statement requirement under section 134(5)(e) applies to every company, whether listed or unlisted, and not merely to listed companies
options.C: For a listed company, the directors must state that they had laid down internal financial controls to be followed by the company, and that such controls were ADEQUATE and were OPERATING EFFECTIVELY; where a failure in the control system occurred during the year (even if subsequently reinstated), the directors CANNOT validly state that controls were adequate and operating effectively, since 'adequate, operating effectively, and applicable throughout' must be read together
options.D: 'Adequate' and 'operating effectively' are treated as synonymous, interchangeable terms under section 134(5)(e), such that satisfying one automatically and necessarily satisfies the other, with no distinct meaning attributable to either term

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) For a listed company, the directors must state that they had laid down internal financial controls to be followed by the company, and that such controls were ADEQUATE and were OPERATING EFFECTIVELY; where a failure in the control system occurred during the year (even if subsequently reinstated), the directors CANNOT validly state that controls were adequate and operating effectively, since 'adequate, operating effectively, and applicable throughout' must be read together

Section 134(5)(e) is a listed-company-specific requirement: 'adequate' addresses whether the control/system design is fit for purpose, while 'operating effectively' addresses whether it actually achieves its risk-mitigating purpose in practice - and both, read together with 'applicable throughout', mean a mid-year control failure (even if later reinstated) precludes directors from validly certifying controls as adequate and operating effectively for that year, exactly as illustrated by the Modern Furniture Limited example in the Study Material.

question_html: If a company is in default of complying with the provisions of section 134, what penalty is prescribed for the company and for every officer of the company who is in default?

options.A: The company shall be liable to a penalty of Rs. 50,000, and every officer of the company who is in default shall be liable to a penalty of Rs. 3,00,000 - i.e., the reverse of the correct company/officer penalty allocation

answer_html:

question_html: A company shall constitute a CSR Committee if, during the immediately preceding financial year, it satisfies which of the following criteria?

options.A: ANY ONE of: net worth of Rs. 500 crore or more; OR turnover of Rs. 1,000 crore or more; OR net profit of Rs. 5 crore or more - satisfying even one of these three alternative thresholds (not necessarily all three) triggers the requirement to constitute a CSR Committee and comply with other CSR provisions

options.C: Only the turnover criterion (Rs. 1,000 crore or more) is relevant for determining CSR applicability; net worth and net profit are not independently relevant criteria under section 135(1)
options.D: A company incurring a loss in the immediately preceding financial year is automatically exempted from CSR applicability, regardless of whether its net worth or turnover independently crosses the prescribed thresholds

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) ANY ONE of: net worth of Rs. 500 crore or more; OR turnover of Rs. 1,000 crore or more; OR net profit of Rs. 5 crore or more - satisfying even one of these three alternative thresholds (not necessarily all three) triggers the requirement to constitute a CSR Committee and comply with other CSR provisions

Section 135(1) uses an 'OR' structure - net worth ≥ Rs. 500 crore, OR turnover ≥ Rs. 1,000 crore, OR net profit ≥ Rs. 5 crore - so satisfying any ONE criterion triggers CSR applicability, as confirmed by the Study Material's own illustration (ABC Ltd., which qualified on turnover alone despite a loss year, since a loss in one preceding year does not affect applicability determined by turnover or net worth).

question_html: What is the standard composition of a CSR Committee, and under what circumstance does section 135(9) dispense with the requirement to constitute one at all?

options.A: The CSR Committee must always consist of exactly five directors, all of whom must be independent directors, with no modified composition available for any category of company under the proviso to section 135(1)
options.B: The standard CSR Committee consists of three or more directors, of whom at least one shall be an independent director (with modified compositions for companies not required to appoint an independent director, private companies with only two directors, and foreign companies); under section 135(9), where the amount to be spent under section 135(5) does NOT EXCEED Rs. 50 lakh, the requirement to constitute a CSR Committee is dispensed with entirely, and the Board of Directors itself discharges the Committee's functions
options.C: Section 135(9) dispenses with the CSR Committee requirement only where the amount to be spent under section 135(5) exceeds (rather than does not exceed) Rs. 50 lakh, this being the threshold for exemption rather than for compulsory constitution
options.D: The CSR Committee, once required to be constituted, can never be dispensed with under any circumstance, regardless of the quantum of CSR amount the company is required to spend in a given financial year

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The standard CSR Committee consists of three or more directors, of whom at least one shall be an independent director (with modified compositions for companies not required to appoint an independent director, private companies with only two directors, and foreign companies); under section 135(9), where the amount to be spent under section 135(5) does NOT EXCEED Rs. 50 lakh, the requirement to constitute a CSR Committee is dispensed with entirely, and the Board of Directors itself discharges the Committee's functions

The standard composition is three-plus directors with at least one independent director (subject to modified compositions for specific categories under the proviso), while section 135(9) provides a small-spend carve-out: where the required CSR spend does not exceed Rs. 50 lakh, no separate Committee is needed and the Board itself performs the Committee's functions.

question_html: What is the minimum CSR spending obligation under section 135(5), and how is it computed for a company that has NOT completed three financial years since its incorporation?

options.A: The minimum CSR spending obligation is a flat 5% of the company's net profit for the CURRENT financial year alone, with no reference at all to average net profits of preceding years, whether three years' worth or fewer
options.B: A company that has not completed three financial years since its incorporation is entirely EXEMPT from any CSR spending obligation, rather than being required to compute the 2% obligation based on such fewer preceding years as are available
options.C: The Board shall ensure the company spends, in every financial year, at least TWO PERCENT of the AVERAGE NET PROFITS made during the THREE immediately preceding financial years; where the company has not completed three financial years since incorporation, it shall spend at least 2% of the average net profits made during SUCH (fewer) immediately preceding financial years as are actually available
options.D: The 2% spending obligation is computed on the company's TURNOVER (rather than average net profits) for the three immediately preceding financial years, regardless of how long the company has been in existence

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The Board shall ensure the company spends, in every financial year, at least TWO PERCENT of the AVERAGE NET PROFITS made during the THREE immediately preceding financial years; where the company has not completed three financial years since incorporation, it shall spend at least 2% of the average net profits made during SUCH (fewer) immediately preceding financial years as are actually available

Section 135(5) fixes the obligation at 2% of average net profits over the three immediately preceding financial years; for a company not yet three years old, the same 2% rate applies to the average net profits of whatever shorter period of preceding financial years is actually available - the obligation is scaled down in the averaging base, not eliminated entirely.

question_html: Besides every listed company, which unlisted PUBLIC companies are required to appoint an internal auditor under Rule 13(1) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014?

options.A: An unlisted public company must satisfy ALL FOUR of the listed thresholds simultaneously (paid-up capital, turnover, outstanding loans, and outstanding deposits) before the requirement to appoint an internal auditor arises under Rule 13(1)
options.B: Internal audit applicability for unlisted public companies is governed solely by turnover, with a threshold of Rs. 500 crore or more; paid-up capital, outstanding loans, and outstanding deposits are not independently relevant criteria under Rule 13(1)
options.C: Unlisted public companies are entirely exempt from the requirement to appoint an internal auditor under section 138 and Rule 13(1); this requirement applies exclusively to listed companies and private companies

What is the closing date of Meridian BioSciences Limited's first financial year, given its incorporation on 20th February, 2026?

options.A: 31st March, 2026 - since every company's financial year must end on 31st March of the same calendar year in which it is incorporated, regardless of the specific date of incorporation within that year
options.B: 28th February, 2027 - since section 2(41) fixes a company's first financial year at exactly twelve months from the date of incorporation, rather than at the following 31st March

options.D: 31st March, 2028 - since section 2(41) allows two full financial years to elapse before the first financial year closes, where a company is incorporated after 1st January of a year

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) 31st March, 2027 - since Meridian BioSciences was incorporated on or after 1st January of a year (20th February, 2026 falling after 1st January 2026), section 2(41) fixes its first financial year as the period ending on 31st March of the FOLLOWING year, i.e., 31st March, 2027, rather than 31st March, 2026

question_html:
Vantage Steel Limited's current financial year is 2026-27. The Income-tax authorities, during an assessment proceeding, discovered indications of fraudulent accounting practices in Vantage Steel's books for the financial year 2016-17, and filed an application before the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) seeking an order to re-open Vantage Steel's books of account and recast its financial statements for that year. Separately, in an unrelated matter, the directors of Vantage Steel have formed the opinion that the company's financial statements for FY 2023-24 (one of the three financial years immediately preceding FY 2026-27) do not comply with section 129, and wish to prepare a revised financial statement for that year on a voluntary basis.

Is the Income-tax authorities' application to the NCLT, seeking re-opening of Vantage Steel Limited's books of account for FY 2016-17, within the time limit prescribed under section 130(3), given that the current financial year is 2026-27?

options.A: Yes - the application is validly within the 8-financial-year limit, since FY 2016-17 falls within the eight financial years immediately preceding the current financial year 2026-27, computed as FY 2016-17 through FY 2023-24
options.B: No - section 130(3) confines a re-opening order to the eight financial years immediately preceding the current financial year; with FY 2026-27 as the current year, the eight preceding years are FY 2018-19 through FY 2025-26, and FY 2016-17 falls OUTSIDE (before) this eight-year window, so an order re-opening FY 2016-17's accounts would not be valid (absent a Central-Government-directed longer preservation period under the proviso to section 128(5))
options.C: Yes - section 130(3) imposes no time limit at all on re-opening applications made by the Income-tax authorities specifically, even though such a limit does apply to applications made by the Central Government, SEBI, or any other person concerned
options.D: No - but only because the application was filed by the Income-tax authorities; had the identical application been filed by the Central Government instead, the 8-financial-year limit under section 130(3) would not have applied at all

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) No - section 130(3) confines a re-opening order to the eight financial years immediately preceding the current financial year; with FY 2026-27 as the current year, the eight preceding years are FY 2018-19 through FY 2025-26, and FY 2016-17 falls OUTSIDE (before) this eight-year window, so an order re-opening FY 2016-17's accounts would not be valid (absent a Central-Government-directed longer preservation period under the proviso to section 128(5))

With FY 2026-27 as the current financial year, the eight financial years immediately preceding it run from FY 2018-19 to FY 2025-26 - FY 2016-17 falls before (outside) this window, so the application to re-open FY 2016-17 exceeds the section 130(3) limit and would not be valid on this ground, exactly as illustrated by the Study Material's own Chetan Ltd. example (where a similarly time-barred application by the Income-tax authorities was held invalid to that extent, notwithstanding that the application itself was validly filed by a competent applicant).

What is the minimum amount Falconbridge Industries Limited is required to spend on CSR activities for FY 2026-27, applying the 2% average-net-profit formula under section 135(5)?

options.A: Rs. 2.4 crore - computed as 2% of the HIGHEST of the three preceding years' net profits (Rs. 120 crore), rather than 2% of their average, i.e., treating the highest single year's profit as the relevant base under section 135(5)
options.B: Rs. 1.2 crore - computed as 2% of the LOWEST of the three preceding years' net profits (Rs. 60 crore), rather than 2% of their average, i.e., treating the lowest single year's profit as the relevant base under section 135(5)
options.C: Rs. 5.4 crore - computed as 2% of the SUM (rather than the average) of the three preceding years' net profits, i.e., 2% of Rs. 270 crore (Rs. 60 crore + Rs. 90 crore + Rs. 120 crore)

answer_html:

options.A: The Rs. 30 lakh, relating to an ongoing project, must be transferred to the Unspent Corporate Social Responsibility Account, within a period of THIRTY DAYS from the end of the financial year (FY 2026-27); it must then be spent in pursuance of the CSR Policy/annual action plan within THREE FINANCIAL YEARS from the date of such transfer, failing which it must be transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII, within thirty days of completion of that third financial year

options.C: The Rs. 30 lakh may simply be carried forward and added to the following year's CSR budget without any requirement to transfer it to a separate Unspent CSR Account or to report the shortfall in the Board's report
options.D: The Rs. 30 lakh must be immediately forfeited to the company's general reserve, since unspent amounts relating to ongoing CSR projects cannot, under any circumstances, be transferred to an Unspent CSR Account or subsequently spent

question_html:
Nordic Apparel Limited is a company listed on a recognised stock exchange in India. For its upcoming Annual General Meeting, Nordic Apparel proposes to circulate copies of its financial statements, auditor's report, and Board's report to its members only FIFTEEN days before the date of the meeting (rather than the ordinarily required twenty-one days). Separately, Nordic Apparel is considering, as an alternative to full circulation, making the documents available for inspection at its registered office and instead sending only a statement of salient features in Form AOC-3 to its members and debenture-trustees.

Can Nordic Apparel Limited validly circulate its financial statements only 15 days (rather than the ordinarily required 21 days) before the AGM, and if so, under what condition?

options.A: Yes, without any need for member consent at all - the 21-day circulation period under section 136(1) is merely a directory (non-mandatory) guideline, and a listed company may unilaterally shorten it to any period it considers convenient
options.B: No - section 136(1) permits shortening the circulation period only for companies having NO share capital, and Nordic Apparel Limited (having share capital) can never validly circulate documents in less than 21 days, under any circumstances
options.C: Yes, but only if the deemed-consent condition under the First Proviso to section 136(1) is satisfied - i.e., if members holding a MAJORITY IN NUMBER entitled to vote, and representing not less than NINETY-FIVE PERCENT of the paid-up share capital giving a right to vote at the meeting, agree to the shorter period; absent such consent, circulation only 15 days before the meeting would not comply with section 136(1)
options.D: Yes, but only if members representing not less than fifty-one percent (a simple majority) of the paid-up share capital giving a right to vote at the meeting agree to the shorter period, rather than the higher ninety-five percent threshold

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Yes, but only if the deemed-consent condition under the First Proviso to section 136(1) is satisfied - i.e., if members holding a MAJORITY IN NUMBER entitled to vote, and representing not less than NINETY-FIVE PERCENT of the paid-up share capital giving a right to vote at the meeting, agree to the shorter period; absent such consent, circulation only 15 days before the meeting would not comply with section 136(1)

The First Proviso to section 136(1) permits circulation in less than 21 days only where deemed consent is obtained: for a company having share capital, this requires a majority in number of members entitled to vote AND holding not less than 95% of the relevant paid-up share capital - a considerably higher bar than a simple 51% majority, and not merely a directory guideline that a listed company may unilaterally waive.

options.B: Yes - the inspection-plus-salient-features route is available unconditionally to every listed company, and a shareholder has no right to insist on receiving the full financial statements even if he specifically requests them
options.C: Yes, but this deemed-compliance route requires the documents to be available for inspection for a period of THIRTY DAYS (not 21 days) before the meeting, and Form AOC-3 must be sent at least THIRTY DAYS (not 21 days) before the meeting
options.D: Yes - the Second Proviso to section 136(1) deems compliance, for a listed company, if the documents are made available for inspection at its registered office during working hours for 21 days before the meeting, AND a statement of salient features in Form AOC-3 (or Form AOC-3A, as applicable) or copies of the documents are sent to every member and trustee for debenture-holders not less than 21 days before the meeting - UNLESS a shareholder specifically asks for the full financial statements, in which case the full statements must be provided to that shareholder

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Yes - the Second Proviso to section 136(1) deems compliance, for a listed company, if the documents are made available for inspection at its registered office during working hours for 21 days before the meeting, AND a statement of salient features in Form AOC-3 (or Form AOC-3A, as applicable) or copies of the documents are sent to every member and trustee for debenture-holders not less than 21 days before the meeting - UNLESS a shareholder specifically asks for the full financial statements, in which case the full statements must be provided to that shareholder

options.A: By 30th September, 2026 itself - section 137(2) requires filing to be completed by the very date on which the AGM should have been held, with no additional 30-day grace period thereafter
options.B: By 30th October, 2026 - section 137(2) requires filing within THIRTY DAYS of the LAST DATE BEFORE WHICH THE AGM SHOULD HAVE BEEN HELD (i.e., 30 days from 30th September, 2026, being the last date by which the AGM should have been held under section 96), together with the duly signed financial statements and a statement of facts and reasons for not holding the AGM
options.C: By 29th March, 2027 - section 137(2) allows filing within one hundred eighty days of the last date before which the AGM should have been held, mirroring the timeline applicable to a One Person Company under section 137(1)
options.D: Crimson Motors Limited has no obligation to file its financial statements with the Registrar at all until the AGM is actually held, however long that may take, since section 137(2) applies only where the AGM has been held but the accounts were not adopted

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) By 30th October, 2026 - section 137(2) requires filing within THIRTY DAYS of the LAST DATE BEFORE WHICH THE AGM SHOULD HAVE BEEN HELD (i.e., 30 days from 30th September, 2026, being the last date by which the AGM should have been held under section 96), together with the duly signed financial statements and a statement of facts and reasons for not holding the AGM

Section 137(2) squarely addresses the AGM-not-held scenario: filing (with duly signed financial statements and a statement of facts/reasons for non-holding of the AGM) must occur within 30 days of the last date before which the AGM should have been held - here, 30 days from 30th September 2026, landing on 30th October 2026 - exactly mirroring the Study Material's own R Ltd. illustration.

Crimson Motors Limited's Annual General Meeting for laying its financial statements for FY 2025-26 was required to be held on or before 30th September, 2026 (per section 96), but the AGM was NOT, in fact, held by that date, and remains un-held as of the date of this question.

Suppose, in a variant of these facts, Crimson Motors Limited's AGM HAD actually been held on 27th September, 2026, but the accounts laid before that AGM were NOT adopted by the shareholders (and no adjourned AGM has yet taken place). Within what time must the un-adopted financial statements be filed with the Registrar, and what status will the Registrar accord to them?

options.A: Within thirty days of the date of the AGM, but the Registrar shall treat such un-adopted financial statements as FINAL and binding, with no need for any subsequent re-filing once the accounts are eventually adopted at an adjourned AGM
options.B: Crimson Motors Limited has no obligation to file anything with the Registrar until the accounts are actually adopted at an adjourned AGM, since section 137(1) does not contemplate filing of UN-adopted financial statements under any circumstance
options.C: Within THIRTY DAYS of the date of the AGM (i.e., by 27th October, 2026) - the un-adopted financial statements, along with the required documents, must be filed under the First Proviso to section 137(1); the Registrar shall take them in his records as PROVISIONAL, until the financial statements are re-filed after their adoption at the adjourned AGM
options.D: Within ninety days (not thirty days) of the date of the AGM, since a longer filing window applies specifically where the financial statements were not adopted, as distinct from the ordinary 30-day window applicable to adopted financial statements

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Within THIRTY DAYS of the date of the AGM (i.e., by 27th October, 2026) - the un-adopted financial statements, along with the required documents, must be filed under the First Proviso to section 137(1); the Registrar shall take them in his records as PROVISIONAL, until the financial statements are re-filed after their adoption at the adjourned AGM

This is the distinct AGM-HELD-but-accounts-NOT-adopted scenario addressed by the First Proviso to section 137(1): un-adopted financial statements must still be filed within 30 days of the AGM date (27th September plus 30 days = 27th October, 2026), and the Registrar records them as PROVISIONAL only, pending their eventual filing (within 30 days of the adjourned AGM, per the Second Proviso) once actually adopted - a materially different route from both the AGM-not-held scenario (Question 1) and a straightforward adopted-at-the-original-AGM scenario.

If Crimson Motors Limited contravenes section 137 and the failure continues for 250 days beyond the first day of default, what is the MAXIMUM aggregate penalty the company itself could be liable for under section 137(3), applying the prescribed daily-continuing-failure cap?

options.A: There is no maximum cap at all on the company's penalty under section 137(3); the penalty of Rs. 10,000 plus Rs. 100 per day of continuing failure accrues without any statutory ceiling, however long the default continues
options.B: The maximum aggregate penalty for the company is Rs. 50,000 (fifty thousand rupees), this being the cap applicable to the managing director and Chief Financial Officer (rather than the company itself) under section 137(3)
options.C: The maximum aggregate penalty for the company is Rs. 10,000 (ten thousand rupees) flat, with no additional daily penalty for continuing failure recognised at all under section 137(3)
options.D: Rs. 2,00,000 (two lakh rupees) - section 137(3) fixes the company's penalty at Rs. 10,000 plus a further Rs. 100 for each day of continuing failure, but this aggregate is SUBJECT TO A MAXIMUM OF Rs. 2,00,000 (two lakh rupees); since 250 days of continuing default (at Rs. 100/day, i.e., Rs. 25,000, plus the initial Rs. 10,000 = Rs. 35,000) would not on its own reach the cap, but the question asks for the MAXIMUM the company could be liable for under the statutory ceiling, which is Rs. 2,00,000 regardless of how many days beyond that point the failure continues

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Rs. 2,00,000 (two lakh rupees) - section 137(3) fixes the company's penalty at Rs. 10,000 plus a further Rs. 100 for each day of continuing failure, but this aggregate is SUBJECT TO A MAXIMUM OF Rs. 2,00,000 (two lakh rupees); since 250 days of continuing default (at Rs. 100/day, i.e., Rs. 25,000, plus the initial Rs. 10,000 = Rs. 35,000) would not on its own reach the cap, but the question asks for the MAXIMUM the company could be liable for under the statutory ceiling, which is Rs. 2,00,000 regardless of how many days beyond that point the failure continues

Section 137(3) fixes the company's penalty at Rs. 10,000 plus Rs. 100 for each day of continuing failure, but expressly caps this aggregate at a MAXIMUM of Rs. 2,00,000 - a separate, lower Rs. 50,000 cap applies to the managing director/CFO (or, in their absence, the responsible director(s)), so the two figures must not be conflated; the company's own liability cannot, in any event, exceed Rs. 2,00,000, however long the continuing failure persists beyond the point that ceiling is reached.
